questions.question: What are zero values in Go?
questions.title: Go Zero Values
questions.direct_answer: Every declared Go variable receives a useful zero value when no initializer is provided: 0 for numbers, false for bool, an empty string for string, and nil for pointers, slices, maps, functions, interfaces, and channels.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand Go's deliberate initialization model.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Reading from a nil map or dereferencing a nil pointer because zero value means allocated.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish a nil slice, which can be appended to, from a nil map, which must be made before writes.

sections.title: What the interviewer wants
sections.content: Define Go Zero Values simply, show a small example, and mention the main trade-off or edge case.

sections.title: Safe defaults
sections.content: Go initializes every variable. The zero value is type-specific and lets many types work without constructors.

sections.title: Zero-value examples
sections.content:
```go
var count int       // 0
var ready bool       // false
var names []string   // nil slice
var scores map[string]int // nil map
```

sections.title: Interview cues
items: Nil slices can be read and appended to.
Nil maps can be read but assigning a key panics; use make.
A zero pointer is nil and cannot be dereferenced.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Go gives every variable a type-specific zero value. That removes uninitialized-memory bugs, but I still distinguish nil from an allocated empty value, especially for maps, slices, pointers, and interfaces.

sections.title: Concept explained
sections.content: Walk through the example step by step, then say when this approach is a good fit and what you would test at the boundary.

followup_questions: How do you safely initialize a map?
